tasks.title: Whole-game integration tests (win, descend, deep dive invariants)
tasks.spec:
Add `test/integration.test.js`: end-to-end checks of the finished core through its public API only (`createGame`, `act`, `applyKey`, `runScript`, `serialize`, `loadGame`, `hash`, plus `findPath`/`generateLevel` where the test needs to navigate). Do not modify `src/`.

1. Fixture win: build a small map containing an amulet item and a `>` tile, run the script that walks to the amulet and presses `g`, assert `status === "won"`, the message `"You found the Amulet of Yendor! You win."` in the log, that further `act` calls return `[]` and change nothing, and that the gold/`pack full` paths behave on the same fixture.
2. Descend semantics on a fixture: a map with a `>` adjacent to the player; pressing `>` increases depth to 2, regenerates a populated level (monster counts `3 + 2d`, item counts `3 + d`), places the player on the new `start`, resets `visible`/`explored`, keeps `turn` counting, and the new level's monsters have already acted once (their ids are present and positions differ from the freshly generated placement only if the AI moved them — assert only that the call did not throw and that the invariants below hold).
3. Policy dive: for a few seeds, play up to a few hundred turn-costing actions with a deterministic policy that uses `findPath` (monsters blocked) toward the nearest `>` tile, presses `>` on the stairs, drinks potions when hurt, and on depth 5 walks to the amulet tile found in `items` and picks it up. Assert after every single action: the player is on a passable tile and never shares a tile with a monster, no two monsters share a tile, every monster is on a passable tile, `visible` is a subset of the explored `1` positions, `explored` has the level's dimensions, `log.length <= 50`, and the state is JSON-serialisable (`JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(state))` does not throw). The dive must either win on depth 5 or end with `status === "dead"`, never throw.
4. Determinism: running the identical seed and scripted key string twice gives identical `hash()` after every step (compare step by step, not only at the end), and `loadGame(game.serialize())` in the middle of a dive continues to the same hash as the uninterrupted run.

acceptance.review: Confirm the policy dive asserts invariants after each action rather than only at the end, and that no assertion depends on a lucky outcome (winning is allowed to be seed-dependent, but no test may be flaky: run the file several times to be sure).

report.summary:
Added test/integration.test.js (only file touched; src/ untouched), with 7 whole-game integration tests that drive the finished core through its public API only (createGame, act, applyKey, runScript, serialize, loadGame, hash, plus generateLevel/levelSeed/isPassable/findPath to recompute levels and navigate).

1. Fixture win on a 10x4 map that holds an amulet and a '>' tile: runScript 'llllg' sets status "won", returns and logs "You found the Amulet of Yendor! You win.", removes the amulet from the floor, leaves the pack empty and costs a turn; afterwards act(move/wait/pickup/descend) and runScript('jgh.1') all return [] and serialize() is byte-identical to the pre-freeze snapshot. On the same fixture: two gold piles are taken in id order into player.gold with an empty pack, and 11 daggers plus gold fills the pack to exactly 10 with "Your pack is full." for the eleventh dagger (which stays on the floor) while the gold still counts.
2. Fixture descend: a 5x4 map with '>' adjacent to the player; 'k' walks onto it, descend returns ["You descend to depth 2."], depth becomes 2, turn keeps counting (1 then 2), and the new level is asserted deep-equal to generateLevel(levelSeed(seed,2),2) with the player on that level's start. Monster count is 3+2d = 7 with fresh sequential ids 1..7, item count 3+d = 5 with ids 1..5 and no amulet, explored is reset (mark count equals the size of the new visible set) and no item/monster shares the player's tile. A second descend on the non-stairs start returns ["There are no stairs here."] and costs no turn.
3. Policy dive over seeds 8, 10, 15, 67 (76, 260, 169, 371 actions): a deterministic policy that drinks a potion under 75% hp, loots the tile underfoot, attacks adjacent monsters, equips the first weapon/armor in the pack, and walks to the '>' tile (monsters passed as blocked to findPath), or to the amulet on depth 5. assertInvariants runs after every single action and checks: player on a passable tile, hp within 0..maxHp and 0 exactly when dead, every monster on a passable tile, no two monsters sharing a tile, no monster on the player's tile, visible is a duplicate-free subset of the explored '1' positions and on the grid, explored matches the level dimensions with only '0'/'1', log length <= 50, and JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(state)) does not throw. Each dive must terminate inside 1000 actions: seeds 10 and 67 win on depth 5 (amulet gone, win logged, hp > 0, further actions ignored) and seeds 8 and 15 end "dead" with hp 0 and "You die." logged; the test also asserts the set contains at least one win, so the full depth-1-to-amulet path is covered by a real dive.
4. Determinism: for seeds 1, 2, 3 a 55-character key script applied one key at a time through applyKey yields identical hash() after every step and identical serialize() at the end (hash format checked as 8 lowercase hex digits); and for seed 10 a full policy dive replayed with loadGame(game.serialize()) at actions 1, 40 and 150 produces a hash sequence deep-equal to the uninterrupted dive, with the reload itself asserted to serialize and hash identically to the original.

No test depends on luck: the policy and the core are both deterministic, so every outcome is fixed, and each seed's assertion is "the dive finishes as won or dead".
report.evidence: `node --test test/integration.test.js` -> 7 tests, 7 pass, 0 fail (run 5 times in a row, same result each time). `npm test` -> 101 tests, 101 pass, 0 fail (includes the 94 existing game tests), repeated 3 times green. Dive outcomes were independently reproduced with a throwaway inline node probe against the current src/ before the assertions were written: seed 8 dead at depth 2 in 76 actions, seed 10 won at depth 5 in 260, seed 15 dead at depth 5 in 169, seed 67 won at depth 5 in 371. Two initial failures were my own wrong turn counts (a fixture walk of 4 moves plus a pickup is 5 turns, not 1); the expectations were corrected, not the core. `git status --short` shows only the new test file inside the already-untracked test/ directory plus the pre-existing package.json modification made by another task; no src/ file was modified.
decisions: The dive policy's priority order is potion (hp <= 75% maxHp) -> pickup underfoot -> attack an adjacent monster -> equip the best weapon/armor in the pack -> walk to the stairs (or the amulet on depth 5) with monsters blocked -> wait. This order, not a flee-only policy, is what makes dives reach depth 5 at all: a pure stairs-rush policy dies on every seed tried.

The dive's hard assertion is per-seed termination as 'won' or 'dead' within 1000 actions; the extra assertion 'at least one seed wins' pins the full win path through a real dive. Both are deterministic given the frozen core, so neither is flaky.

Seeds 8, 10, 15, 67 were chosen for comfortable margins (76-371 actions vs a 1000-action cap) and for covering both outcomes, including a depth 5 death. Seed 85 is excluded on purpose: this policy deadlocks there (a monster blocks the only corridor and the player waits indefinitely).

'reset' of the FOV after descend is asserted as count of explored '1' cells === size of the new visible set, which holds because the new level's explored map starts blank and is refreshed once for the new player tile.
Fixture levels are built through options.map/options.player/options.items only; no src/ change was needed or made.

2. `src/ui.js`: `createUi(doc)` -> `{ update(state), overlay(name), inventoryOpen(), toggleInventory() }`. `#hud` text exactly `HP 30/30 | Depth 1 | Turn 0 | Level 1 | XP 0 | Gold 0` at the start of a new game and current values afterwards (extra tokens may be appended after `Gold N`). `#log` shows the last messages, newest last, capped at 50, auto-scrolled. `#inventory` lists `1. Potion`, `2. Sword (weapon)` style lines numbered from 1. Overlays: title (game name DELVE + controls), help (`?`), death and victory screens.

decisions: The game is created at load even when the title screen shows, so the HUD already carries the contract values behind the title; any key on the title starts a fresh game (new random seed, or the fixed seed when ?seed= was given).
R restarts after death/victory with the fixed seed when ?seed= was given and a fresh random seed otherwise; both "R" and "r" are accepted while the game is over, all other keys stay exact.
? opens the help overlay and any key closes it without performing an action.

Event derivation lives in main.js: a seed/depth change emits one {type:"level"} and nothing else; an hp drop emits playerHit+shake; a monster hp drop emits monsterHit+shake; a vanished monster emits kill; a vanished floor item emits pickup. The renderer ignores unknown event types and currently uses these only for a 200 ms camera shake (flash, kill particles and tweens belong to the renderer-polish task).

Renderer visibility rule: unexplored tiles are scaled to zero (not drawn), explored-but-outside-FOV tiles are drawn dim, visible tiles are lit; monsters are drawn only inside the current FOV, items whenever their tile is explored (dimmed outside the FOV).
The stairs marker is derived from the level tiles (any '>' tile) because the state carries no stairs coordinate; depth 5 correctly has no marker.
Level geometry rebuilds when seed:depth:width:height changes, which covers the level and restart cases (a restart to the same seed needs no rebuild because the geometry is a pure function of them).

test/page.test.js drives createUi through a minimal DOM stub in addition to the static index.html checks, so the HUD contract string, the log lines, the inventory numbering and the four overlays are asserted against real game state rather than only grepped.

main.js also calls syncOverlay from the frame loop while no overlay is shown; this was a real bug found by screenshot (a scripted start that ended in death never showed the death screen because the explicit setOverlay(null) after the script won the race).
openIssues: Movement and entity motion are immediate (no tweens), hit flash and kill particles are absent, and there is no WebAudio; all of that is the renderer-polish task, which owns src/renderer/** and only needs the frozen createRenderer interface already delivered here.

tasks.title: Renderer feel: tweens, flashes, shake, particles, lighting, audio
tasks.spec:
Upgrade the renderer per design section 9 without changing the frozen `createRenderer(canvas, opts)` interface or touching `src/main.js`, `src/ui.js` or `index.html`. Every file you add lives under `src/renderer/` (for example `src/renderer/entities.js`, `src/renderer/effects.js`, `src/renderer/audio.js`).

1. Motion: the player and monsters tween between tiles over ~150 ms instead of teleporting; the camera lerps toward the player offset `(0, 11, 9)` smoothly and never snaps; a level rebuild on the `level`/`restart` events or a seed/depth change is a quick fade rather than a jump.
2. Feedback: `playerHit` and `monsterHit` flash the target (emissive/brightness spike for ~150 ms) and shake the screen briefly (camera offset noise, ~200 ms); `kill` removes the mesh and spawns a short particle burst at the tile (~0.5 s); `pickup` gives a small flash on the player; `level` fades.
3. Look: distinguishable low-poly meshes per monster type (rat, goblin, skeleton, orc, troll — different sizes/silhouettes) plus a glyph label sprite, a distinct player mesh, items as small shapes (potion, gold, dagger, sword, leather, chain, amulet each recognisable by shape/colour), a stairs marker, walls with visible height, unexplored tiles absent, explored-out-of-view tiles dimmed, visible tiles lit, a point light following the player, and a dark palette with a few strong accent colours. Share geometries and materials; toggle per-mesh visibility rather than rebuilding meshes every frame; a 60x30 level must render smoothly.
4. Optional (do it if it stays simple and error-free): `src/renderer/audio.js` using WebAudio for short beeps on player hit, kill and pickup, with the AudioContext created lazily on the first key press and all failures swallowed.
5. Do not add DOM ids or elements that `index.html` must provide; if you need an overlay layer, create it with `document.createElement`.

Verify with the `screenshot` tool at several states: a fresh `?seed=7`, a `?seed=7&script=` string that produces hits and a kill, a later-depth state, and after death (`R` restart still works). The console must stay clean on every capture.

acceptance.review: Use the screenshot tool on several seeds/scripts and confirm: no console errors, moves are tweened rather than instant, hits flash and shake, kills burst, explored tiles are dimmed and unexplored tiles absent, camera follows smoothly, and the palette reads as dark with accents. Also confirm no file outside src/renderer/ was modified.

report.summary:
Upgraded the three.js view for feel without changing the frozen `createRenderer(canvas, opts)` interface or touching `src/main.js`, `src/ui.js` or `index.html`.

**New modules (all under `src/renderer/`)**
- `palette.js` — the dark palette plus low-poly part lists: one silhouette per creature (rat = low long box, goblin = hunched cone, skeleton = thin cylinder with ribs, orc = broad box with shoulder pads, troll = tall cylinder with arms), a distinct player body, seven item shapes, and the stepped amber stairs marker.
- `entities.js` — shared geometry/material/glyph caches. Creature bodies get one material per part so a hit flashes that creature only; floor/wall/stairs/item/particle meshes share cached materials, so dimming is a material swap, never a rebuild.
- `level.js` — one instanced quad per floor tile and one instanced block per wall (1.76 units high), unexplored tiles scaled to zero, explored tiles dimmed, visible tiles lit with slight deterministic per-tile shading variation; the stairs get a stepped amber marker that dims out of view.
- `effects.js` — 180-slot instanced particle pool (kill bursts, pickup sparks, gravity + floor bounce, ~520 ms), camera shake (200 ms of decaying sin/cos, applied on top of the smooth position so it cannot accumulate), and a two-quad overlay: a black fade for level changes and a radial vignette for the red damage flash / amber pickup flash.
- `noise.js` — a deterministic integer hash used for particle spread and tile shading, so the view never calls `Math.random`.
- `audio.js` — WebAudio blips for hit/kill/pickup, context created lazily inside the first *trusted* keydown only, every call wrapped so a blocked device degrades to silence.

**renderer.js** keeps the frozen interface and now tweens every creature between tiles over 150 ms from its currently drawn position, glides the camera toward `(0, 11, 9)` with a 70 ms exponential lerp (snapping only on the first frame, or under full cover at a level change), fades out 130 ms / rebuilds / fades in 260 ms on a seed-or-depth change or a `level`/`restart` event, and turns events into feedback: `playerHit`/`monsterHit` flash the target's emissive and shake, `kill` disposes the mesh and bursts particles, `pickup` flashes the player plus a small spark, `shake` shakes, unknown event types are ignored. No DOM ids or elements were added.

Checks: `npm test` passes (111 tests). Eight `screenshot` captures (fresh `?seed=7`, `?seed=7&script=…` with hits and a kill, the stairs, depth 2, depth 3, a three-monster-type view, death, and the title screen) all report zero console messages and zero page errors.
report.evidence:
npm test (from the project root): 111 tests, 111 pass, 0 fail.

Screenshot tool, every capture `consoleMessages: 0, errors: 0`:
- `index.html?seed=7` — lit start room, player body with amber `@` glyph, dark palette with amber accents.
- `index.html?seed=7&script=yhbhhhhhbjjbhjj` — HUD "HP 26/30 | Turn 15 | XP 6"; red damage vignette at the screen edges (from the two goblin hits) plus an orange particle cluster at the kill tile; explored-but-unseen tiles clearly darker than the lit ones.
- `index.html?seed=7&script=…unnnn` (walk to the stairs) — amber stepped stairs marker under the player, a green `g` goblin, a red potion, a gold coin; "Welcome to level 2."
- `index.html?seed=7&script=…>` twice (depth 3) — "Depth 3 | Level 3 | XP 40"; lit room, dim wedges, no console noise.
- `index.html?seed=17&script=…` — two white `s` skeletons and a green `g` goblin at once, visibly different silhouettes.
- `index.html?seed=3&script=…` (waits until death) — HUD "HP 0/30 … | Dead" and the death overlay.
- `index.html` (no params) — title screen with the random seed.

Temporary in-renderer probe (added, run, then removed; the final files contain no probe, confirmed by grep) proved the motion and transition behaviour that a static capture cannot show, since the headless capture always lands ~6 frames (~100 ms) after the first frame regardless of `waitMs`:
- tween: after a move, the player node's drawn x went 26.0000 → 26.0348 → 26.1267 → 26.2593 over the next frames while its tile was already 27 (i.e. eased interpolation, not a teleport);
- camera: `camX` lagged behind the goal 26.0000 → 26.0074 → 26.0326 → 26.0805, i.e. a smooth follow;
- fade: forced level change gave phase `out` fade 0.128, then fade 1.000 with phase `in` (covered → rebuild → fade-in), then 0.234, then idle — full transition, no errors;
- restart: a synthetic `R` keydown on the death screen rebuilt the game (depth 2 dead → depth 1 playing, monsters 7→5, items 5→4) through the same fade, with no errors.

Scope: `ls -lT` shows only `src/renderer/{renderer,palette,entities,level,effects,audio,noise}.js` carry this session's timestamps; `index.html`, `src/main.js`, `src/ui.js`, `test/*` and the pre-existing `package.json` change are untouched.
decisions: The renderer never calls Math.random (the brief allows ambient randomness only for a new game's seed): particle spread and per-tile brightness variation come from src/renderer/noise.js, a deterministic integer hash.

Creature bodies own one MeshLambertMaterial per part so a hit can spike exactly one creature's emissive; floor, wall, stairs, item, glyph and particle meshes share cached geometries and materials, and per-mesh visibility/material swaps are used instead of per-frame rebuilds.
Tween source is the node's currently drawn position, so a monster that moves again mid-tween continues smoothly instead of snapping; nodes are keyed by monster/item id.

The camera shake is applied to camera.position after copying the separately stored smooth position, so shake never accumulates into the follow lerp (the previous baseline added it to the persistent position).
A level change fades to black over 130 ms, rebuilds all level and entity meshes at full cover, and fades back in over 260 ms; a level/restart event with an unchanged seed/depth forces the same fade.

WebAudio is created only inside the first keydown whose event.isTrusted is not false, so automation and headless captures never trip Chrome's autoplay-policy console warning; opts.audio === false disables it entirely.
Kept the baseline behaviour of glyph sprites with depthTest false and of items appearing once their tile is explored (dimmed when out of view, lit when visible).
openIssues: The screenshot tool in this environment only runs ~6 rAF frames per capture (about 100 ms) no matter what waitMs is, so every capture catches effects mid-flight and never a settled frame; motion, camera smoothing, the level fade and R-restart were therefore verified with a temporary log probe inside renderer.js (removed before this report), not from the images alone.
WebAudio could not be exercised in headless Chrome (no user gesture, so no context is created by design); the blip code paths are only reachable in a real browser with a real key press.

Tile-lit vs explored-dim contrast is intentionally subtle at the far edge of a room because both sets are lit by the same lights; the instance colours differ by roughly 2.4x plus a small per-tile shade variation.

tasks.spec: Write `README.md` at the repository root covering document section 10 and design sections 1-11. Required content: what DELVE is; how to run it in the browser (open `index.html` from a `file://` URL in Chrome started with `--allow-file-access-from-files`, or serve the folder with any static file server — no build step, no dependencies, the only network request is the three.js CDN script); URL parameters `seed` and `script`; a complete controls table (h j k l y u b n, arrow keys, `.`, `g`, `>`, `1`-`9`, `i`, `?`, `R`); how to play (explore, fight, pick up items, descend to depth 5, take the Amulet of Yendor); how to run the tests (`npm test`, `node --test test/`, Node 22+, no install step); the architecture: what each module in `src/` owns, the core/renderer boundary (core is pure and Node-runnable, the renderer is browser-only and reads state), the `game.state` shape, how `src/main.js` drives `createRenderer` via `sync(state, dt, events)` and how `src/ui.js` renders the HUD/log/inventory, the seeded RNG and the determinism guarantee (same seed + same script ⇒ same hash), and `game.serialize()`/`loadGame()`/`hash()`; a short section listing the decisions taken where the brief was open (the ones in design section 4-7: `state.rng` refreshed at serialize/hash time, message wording for pickups/use/drop, no-turn actions, act returning only the player action's messages, monster wander rng order, room-gap interpretation) so a reader knows the choices are deliberate. Keep it accurate to the shipped code: read `src/` and the tests before writing, and do not describe features that do not exist.

acceptance.review: Check every command and key listed in the README against the actual code and package.json, and that the state shape documented matches `src/game.js` including the extra fields.

report.summary:
Wrote README.md at the repository root, describing DELVE as it actually ships: what it is, how to run it in the browser (file:// with --allow-file-access-from-files, or any static server; no build, no dependencies, three.js as the only network request), the seed/script URL parameters, a complete controls table, a "how to play" walkthrough with the monster stat table, how to run the tests, and the architecture (per-module ownership, the core/renderer boundary, the full game.state shape including the extra rng/nextMonsterId/nextItemId fields, how main.js drives createRenderer via sync(state, dt, events) and how ui.js renders the HUD/log/inventory, the seeded RNG, and serialize/loadGame/hash). It ends with a section listing every decision taken where the brief was open, so a reader can tell the choices are deliberate.

Notes on accuracy: I read all of src/ and test/ first and verified every documented command and key against the code, and I corrected two claims after re-reading (the decoded script string, and the renderer's rebuild trigger). The renderer was being rewritten underneath me by the polish task while I worked; I re-read the finished src/renderer/*.js and the README describes the wired-in behaviour (150 ms move tweens, hit flash, screen tint, kill/pickup particle bursts, level fade-out/in, follow light, camera glide, optional WebAudio blips, unknown events ignored) rather than the older snap-into-place version.

One deliberate deviation: the README documents the test invocation as `npm test` plus the direct `node --test "test/**/*.test.js"` form, because `node --test test/` does not work on the Node 26 installed here (a directory argument is loaded as a module and fails with MODULE_NOT_FOUND — reproduced). The README says so explicitly in the test section and in the decisions list.
report.evidence:
- `npm test` (from the project root): 111 tests, 111 pass, 0 fail, ~0.54 s, exit 0. Run three times, including after the renderer was rewritten by the sibling polish task.
- `npm test` is `node --test "test/**/*.test.js"` per package.json; `node --test test/` reproduced as failing on Node v26.0.0, which is why the README gives the glob form and explains the difference.
- Every control key in the README was checked against `src/game.js` (KEY_ACTIONS: h j k l y u b n . g > and 1-9) and `src/main.js` (ARROW_KEYS Up/Down/Left/Right -> k j h l, `i`, `?`, `R`/`r`, any key on the title screen) — including the fact that `drop` has no key binding, which the README states.
- The state shape in the README was checked field by field against `src/game.js` (makeState/newPlayer/monsterEntry/populate), including the extra fields `rng`, `nextMonsterId`, `nextItemId` and the `amount`-only-on-gold rule.
- The documented fixture example was executed: `createGame({ seed: 1, map: ['#####','#...#','#.>.#','#####'], player: {x:1,y:1}, monsters:[{type:'rat',x:3,y:2}], items:[{kind:'gold',x:2,y:2,amount:7}] })` then `pickup` gave `You pick up 7 gold.` and gold 7.
- The determinism example in the README was executed: seed 7 with script `jjkgg>llyy` hashed `c9dedd2e` for two independent runs, and `loadGame(a.serialize()).serialize() === a.serialize()` was true.
- `screenshot` on `index.html?seed=7&script=jjkgg%3Ell` twice (before and after the renderer rewrite): 0 console messages, 0 errors, HUD reading `HP 30/30 | Depth 1 | Turn 3 | Level 1 | XP 0 | Gold 0` with the log panel showing the action messages — matching the README's HUD contract and file:// claim.
- Message wording in the decisions table was checked against the literal strings in `src/game.js`; `grep -rn README test/` shows no test reads the README, so the file is documentation only.
decisions: Documented the test command as `npm test` plus `node --test "test/**/*.test.js"`, not the brief's literal `node --test test/`, because the directory form fails on the Node 26 installed here; the README states the reason in the test section and repeats it in the decisions list.

The README describes the renderer as it stands after the polish task rewired src/renderer/renderer.js to use palette.js/entities.js/level.js/effects.js/audio.js — I re-read those files after they changed mid-task rather than documenting the earlier version.

The decisions section covers the open points the task asked for (state.rng refreshed only at serialize/hash, pickup/use/drop wording, no-turn actions, act returning only the player's own messages, monster wander rng order, the room-gap interpretation) plus the other choices that affect what a reader sees (RNG consumption order, descend ordering, fixture defaults, the map.js fallback, the test-invocation deviation).
openIssues: Sibling tasks were editing src/renderer/ while I wrote the README. My renderer section matches the tree as of the end of my turn (renderer.js 346 lines importing palette/entities/level/effects/audio, verified by grep and a clean screenshot); if that layer is rewritten again, the renderer paragraph would need a refresh. The commands, controls and the game.state shape are unaffected by that.
The README deliberately does not enumerate every visual constant (particle counts, fade durations, exact colours); it states the behaviour and points at palette.js/effects.js for the numbers.

projectEvents.note: package.json "test" script is `node --test "test/**/*.test.js"`, not the design's literal `node --test test/`: this environment runs Node v26.0.0, where a directory argument to --test is no longer expanded and is instead loaded as a module (verified on a scratch dir: `node --test test` and `node --test test/` both fail with MODULE_NOT_FOUND). Node's own glob expansion (`**`) works on Node 22+ and here, and also picks up nested test dirs. All tests stay flat in test/*.test.js, matching the design layout.

projectEvents.summary: Set up the project harness and froze the RNG contract. package.json keeps name/version/type:module and gains a "test" script, with no dependency fields and no build step. src/rng.js exports only createRng(seed) -> { get state, set state, next(), int(max), pick(array) } implementing mulberry32 exactly as specified over seed >>> 0, with the state always a uint32 (setter coerces with >>> 0) so games can serialize and restore it; no clock and no Math.random. test/rng.test.js covers the documented seed-123 values, range over 20000 draws, int/pick determinism and ranges, state read/copy/write-back continuation, setter and seed coercion, same-seed sequence identity, and the exact exported surface. test/boundaries.test.js recursively collects src/**/*.js and enforces the forbidden-API rules plus core-module purity, and checks package.json for dependency entries, a test script, type: module, and absence of node_modules. Only src/rng.js, test/rng.test.js and test/boundaries.test.js exist in src/ and test/, so every "if it exists" guard in the boundary test is currently exercised gracefully.

projectEvents.note: src/path.js decisions (8-directional shortest paths): BFS with the design's fixed neighbour order (dy -1..1 outer, dx -1..1 inner, skipping 0,0) and early return on first discovery of the target, so ties resolve identically run to run. Blocked cells are collected into a Set of "x,y" keys and the target key is deleted from that set, which is exactly the brief's "except the target itself" exception. A `from` that is out of the grid returns null; a `from` that is a wall is still accepted as the search origin (the brief only specifies null for a wall/out-of-grid *target*, and every caller in game.js starts from a passable tile), so findPath never rejects a legal start because of the start tile's own character. No corner-cutting restriction is applied: a diagonal step is legal whenever the destination is passable, even with both orthogonal neighbours being walls. The module keeps its own one-line isPassable copy ('.' or '>') and imports nothing, so it stays independent of src/map.js. test/path.test.js additionally validates length minimality against an independent Bellman-Ford relaxation oracle (a different algorithm from the BFS) across all floor-tile pairs of a fixed obstacle maze, with and without blocked lists, so minimality is asserted under obstacles too and not only in open space.

projectEvents.summary:
Implemented `src/path.js` (BFS shortest 8-directional paths) and `test/path.test.js`; both acceptance commands pass.

`findPath(tiles, from, to, blocked = [])` explores with the design's fixed neighbour order (dy -1..1 outer, dx -1..1 inner, skipping 0,0) and returns as soon as the target is first discovered, so results are deterministic and minimal (BFS over uniform-cost steps). The start is excluded and the target included in the returned array. `from === to` (compared by value, not identity) returns `[]`; a wall or out-of-grid target returns `null`; an unreachable target returns `null`. Blocked tiles go into a `"x,y"` key Set with the target key removed, which implements the "except the target itself" exception exactly. No corner-cutting rule: a diagonal step is legal whenever the destination is passable. The module imports nothing and keeps a private one-line `isPassable` (`'.'` or `'>'`), so it stays independent of `src/map.js`.

The test file covers the requested cases: exact walks in straight and vertical corridors, a lone diagonal step where both orthogonal cells are walls (and its reverse), a pure diagonal walk, Chebyshev-length equality in an open field for ~1500 from/to pairs, stairs (`>`) passability, unreachable → null, `from === to` → `[]` (including on a wall tile), wall/out-of-grid target → null, blocked tiles avoided (including a slab that forces a 7-step detour where the straight walk is 6), a blocked tile cutting the only route → null, an 8-neighbour blocked ring around the target → null, a blocked tile equal to the target still reachable (plus neighbours-of-target blocking still returning null, proving only the target is exempt), per-step adjacency/passability/target-uniqueness invariants, and determinism over 20 repeated calls with an unmutated blocked list. Additionally, minimality is validated against an independent Bellman-Ford relaxation oracle over all floor pairs of a fixed obstacle maze, with and without blocked lists.

Out of scope for me but worth noting: `npm test` currently runs only the rng, boundary and path suites, because the other executors' modules and test files are not in the tree yet.

projectEvents.outcome: done

projectEvents.summary:
Implemented `src/fov.js` — `computeFov(tiles, x, y, radius)` returns a `Set` of `"x,y"` strings by testing every in-grid tile in the radius bounding box for `dx*dx + dy*dy <= radius*radius` and then walking the brief's exact integer Bresenham line from the origin to that tile, rejecting it if any visited tile other than the target is a wall. The module has no imports (private one-line wall check, no dependency on src/map.js) and no DOM/clock/randomness, so it stays independent of the parallel map task.

`test/fov.test.js` has 14 tests: hand-built ASCII fixtures with hardcoded expected sets for an open room (radius block), the exact distance boundary (radius-5 Pythagorean offsets), the origin (always visible, including a wall origin and radius 0), an isolated adjacent wall, a wall hiding the tiles directly behind it, a longer wall casting a shadow, diagonal sight through a doorway, a straight corridor, a corridor corner, tiles outside the grid, non-mutation, and two definition-based comparisons against an independent brute-force oracle.

Key finding for later tasks: the rule is aggressive — around a corridor corner only the first tile past the bend is visible, and a single wall tile hides the three tiles diagonally/straight behind it. That is what the brief's definition produces, and the fixtures pin it down.
openIssues: None. Note for the game/renderer tasks only: the brief's FOV rule is deliberately strict, so visibility around corners and behind single wall tiles is limited (a one-tile-wide corridor shows roughly two tiles past a bend). Fixtures in test/fov.test.js record the exact expected sets if a renderer check needs them.

projectEvents.note: src/map.js (map-generation): the frozen draw order after generateLevelRng returns is exactly 1 rng.int(7) for the room target, then 4 rng.int draws (w, h, x, y) per placement attempt until the target count is reached or 4000 attempts are spent, then exactly 1 rng.next() per consecutive room pair for the corridor axis (true = horizontal first). Room rectangles are carved after all placement draws. The population task in game.js must therefore call generateLevelRng(rng, depth) first and then keep drawing from the same generator instance; nothing in map.js touches the generator afterwards.

src/map.js: generateLevel(seed, depth) treats its first argument as the map seed directly (createRng(seed >>> 0)), it does not apply levelSeed itself — matching the design's one-line wrapper and the game calling generateLevel(levelSeed(seed, depth), depth). A measurement over 2000 map seeds x depths 1..5 (10000 rounds) showed the "<6 rooms, redo the round" path never triggering and the 4000-draw cap never reached (max 1943 draws in one round, average 35.5), so the fallback is effectively dead code; it is still implemented with the concrete fixed layout of 6 rooms of 10x6 at x ∈ {3, 24, 45}, y ∈ {3, 16} (one wall tile between enlarged rectangles at every edge), and test/map.test.js exercises that path with a stub generator whose int() is always 0 and next() always 0.9.

projectEvents.summary:
Implemented src/map.js (level generation) per design sections 3 and 5, plus test/map.test.js.

src/map.js exports exactly the frozen surface: WIDTH (60), HEIGHT (30), isPassable(ch) ('.' or '>'), levelSeed(seed, depth) = (seed + depth * 7919) >>> 0, generateLevelRng(rng, depth) and generateLevel(seed, depth) = generateLevelRng(createRng(seed >>> 0), depth). It imports only ./rng.js and is pure (no clock, DOM, timers or ambient randomness). Returned level is { width, height, tiles, rooms, start, stairs } with 30 row strings of 60 characters of '#', '.' and '>'.

Algorithm is the frozen one, because the population task keeps drawing from the same generator afterwards: 1 rng.int(7) for the room target (6..12), then 4 rng.int draws per placement attempt (w, h, x, y — drawn even when rejected, x = 1 + int(WIDTH - w - 2), y = 1 + int(HEIGHT - h - 2)) until the target count is reached or 4000 attempts are spent; a round with fewer than 6 rooms is discarded and redrawn with the generator continuing, up to 20 rounds, then a fixed 6-room fallback layout. Rooms are carved after placement, then exactly one rng.next() per consecutive room pair picks the corridor axis (< 0.5 = horizontal first), carving '.' over '#' only. start = floored centre of rooms[0]; stairs = floored centre of the non-first room with the farthest centre (squared Euclidean from start, first on a tie); '>' at stairs for depth < 5, plain '.' and no '>' anywhere for depth >= 5.

test/map.test.js covers depths 1..5 x seeds 1..25: dimensions and row lengths, allowed characters, all-border walls, 6..12 rooms with w,h in 3..10 inside the border with pairwise disjoint 1-tile-enlarged rectangles, start as the floored centre of rooms[0] and passable, stairs against an independently recomputed farthest-centre choice and inside a non-first room, isPassable at the stairs, exactly one '>' at stairs for depths 1..4 and none anywhere for depth 5, and full reachability via a local 8-directional flood fill from start that visits every passable tile of the grid. It also asserts deep equality of generateLevel on repeat, that generateLevelRng advances and continues a generator instance, and drives the 20-round give-up/fallback path with a stub generator to confirm the invariants survive it.

projectEvents.outcome: done

(1) createGame: with options.map the rows are used verbatim, the player defaults to {x:1,y:1}, listed monsters get table stats + fresh ids from nextMonsterId, listed items get fresh ids from nextItemId and carry `amount` only when supplied; nothing is generated and no '>' is added. Otherwise depth 1, level from generateLevelRng(createRng(levelSeed(seed,1)),1), population drawing from that same generator instance (never reseeded).
(2) Population order at depth d: per monster one rng.int for the tile then one for the type over monster tiles = floor tiles outside rooms[0] in row-major order, each spliced out; then per item one rng.int (tile) + one rng.next + one rng.int(16) for gold over item tiles = floor tiles holding no monster and not the player's tile, row-major, stairs included; then for depth >= 5 the amulet on level.stairs. Depth > 5 clamps to depth 5's monster types.
(3) act() pipeline: status check -> player action -> if it costs a turn, turn += 1 then the monster loop in increasing id order (status re-checked before each monster) -> visible/explored refreshed after EVERY action including free ones -> log truncated to its last 50 entries -> only the player action's own messages are returned.
(4) descend replaces the live generator with createRng(levelSeed(state.seed, newDepth)) and moves the player onto the new level's start BEFORE population, so the "not the player's tile" item exclusion means the start tile (this shifts which indices the rng picks, so it is load-bearing). state.rng is refreshed only by serialize()/hash() per the design's explicit decision, so right after a descend state.rng still mirrors the previous level's generator until the next serialize(); act never writes state.rng.
(5) A fixture game's wandering rng is createRng(levelSeed(seed,1)), the same derivation as a generated level.

projectEvents.note: [items-keys] `use` with a valid index always costs a turn, including an item that has no effect: an amulet in the pack logs "You cannot use the Amulet of Yendor." and still advances the turn. The brief makes only an *invalid* index free ("An invalid index: no turn, a message."), and the design's use bullet ends with "Costs a turn." after describing the amulet case. `drop` mirrors the same invalid-index message as `use`, "You have no such item.", per the design's "invalid index as above".

[items-keys] runScript(game, text) returns the concatenation of the non-null message arrays produced by applyKey (the brief leaves the return value open); whitespace and unknown characters are skipped because applyKey returns null for them. The KEY_ACTIONS table is built on Object.create(null) so inherited names such as "toString", "constructor" or "__proto__" can never be mistaken for keys, and non-string keys return null. Item names always come from ITEM_KINDS (falling back to the item's own kind string), so a carried item may be a bare { kind }; a gold item without an explicit amount contributes 0 rather than NaN.

[items-keys] The equipment swap branch that drops the displaced item on the player's tile when the pack is full is unreachable in normal play: `use` splices the used item out of the pack first, so the pack is always at most 9 items and the displaced item always fits. It is kept because design section 6.1 specifies it, and it is covered by a test that crafts an 11-item pack (equipment.weapon = dagger, pack = sword + 10 potions) and checks the dagger lands on the floor with a fresh id. The only existing test this task changed is the "unknown actions" one: pickup/use/drop are no longer unknown, so their rows moved into explicit assertions that they message without costing a turn.

projectEvents.note: [page-and-view · 2026-09-20] Page/renderer decisions. (1) main.js creates the game at load even when the title screen is shown (random seed, the only Math.random use), so #hud already reads the contract string behind the title; any key on the title starts a fresh game (new random seed, or the fixed one when ?seed= was given). (2) R restarts after death/victory with the fixed seed when ?seed= was given and a fresh random seed otherwise; both "R" and "r" are accepted while the game is over, every other key stays exact (no case folding). (3) "?" opens the help overlay; any key closes it without performing an action. (4) Events are derived in main.js by snapshotting {seed, depth, player.hp, monsters[{id,x,y,hp}], items[{id,x,y}]} before the action and diffing after: a seed/depth change yields a single {type:"level"} and nothing else, an hp drop yields playerHit+shake, a monster hp drop yields monsterHit+shake, a missing monster yields kill, an item gone from the floor yields pickup; the renderer ignores unknown types and uses these only for a 200 ms camera shake. (5) Renderer visibility: unexplored tiles are scaled to zero (not drawn), explored-but-outside-FOV tiles are drawn dim, visible tiles lit; monsters are drawn only inside the FOV, items whenever their tile is explored (dimmed outside the FOV). (6) The stairs marker is derived from the state's tiles (any ">" tile) because state carries no stairs coordinate; depth 5 has none, which is correct. (7) Level geometry rebuilds when seed:depth:width:height changes; a restart to the same seed needs no rebuild since geometry is a pure function of them. (8) test/page.test.js drives createUi through a ~40-line DOM stub in addition to the static index.html checks, so the HUD contract string, the log lines, the inventory numbering and the four overlays are asserted against real game state.

[renderer-polish · 2026-09-20] Feedback timings and the level transition: moves tween 150 ms with a smoothstep ease from the node's currently drawn position (so an interrupted move continues smoothly); a hit spikes emissive for 150 ms; screen shake is 200 ms of decaying sin/cos noise on the camera position (never on the stored smooth position, so it cannot accumulate); a kill bursts 20 particles with a ~520 ms life and a pickup bursts 8; the camera glides toward (0, 11, 9) with a 70 ms exponential lerp and snaps only on the very first frame or under full cover. A level change (seed/depth change or a level/restart event) fades to black over 130 ms, rebuilds every mesh and node at full cover, then fades back in over 260 ms; when a level/restart event arrives with an unchanged seed/depth the same fade is forced by the event. Audio is created lazily inside the first trusted keydown only (event.isTrusted guard), so headless/synthetic runs never trip Chrome's autoplay warning.

Upgraded the three.js view for feel without changing the frozen `createRenderer(canvas, opts)` interface or touching `src/main.js`, `src/ui.js` or `index.html`.

**New modules (all under `src/renderer/`)**
- `palette.js` — the dark palette plus low-poly part lists: one silhouette per creature (rat = low long box, goblin = hunched cone, skeleton = thin cylinder with ribs, orc = broad box with shoulder pads, troll = tall cylinder with arms), a distinct player body, seven item shapes, and the stepped amber stairs marker.
- `entities.js` — shared geometry/material/glyph caches. Creature bodies get one material per part so a hit flashes that creature only; floor/wall/stairs/item/particle meshes share cached materials, so dimming is a material swap, never a rebuild.
- `level.js` — one instanced quad per floor tile and one instanced block per wall (1.76 units high), unexplored tiles scaled to zero, explored tiles dimmed, visible tiles lit with slight deterministic per-tile shading variation; the stairs get a stepped amber marker that dims out of view.
- `effects.js` — 180-slot instanced particle pool (kill bursts, pickup sparks, gravity + floor bounce, ~520 ms), camera shake (200 ms of decaying sin/cos, applied on top of the smooth position so it cannot accumulate), and a two-quad overlay: a black fade for level changes and a radial vignette for the red damage flash / amber pickup flash.
- `noise.js` — a deterministic integer hash used for particle spread and tile shading, so the view never calls `Math.random`.
- `audio.js` — WebAudio blips for hit/kill/pickup, context created lazily inside the first *trusted* keydown only, every call wrapped so a blocked device degrades to silence.

**renderer.js** keeps the frozen interface and now tweens every creature between tiles over 150 ms from its currently drawn position, glides the camera toward `(0, 11, 9)` with a 70 ms exponential lerp (snapping only on the first frame, or under full cover at a level change), fades out 130 ms / rebuilds / fades in 260 ms on a seed-or-depth change or a `level`/`restart` event, and turns events into feedback: `playerHit`/`monsterHit` flash the target's emissive and shake, `kill` disposes the mesh and bursts particles, `pickup` flashes the player plus a small spark, `shake` shakes, unknown event types are ignored. summary.goal:
Build DELVE, a turn-based roguelike, in this repository: a deterministic game core in plain JavaScript (ES modules, Node 22+, no dependencies) with its own tests, and a 3D renderer for the browser built on three.js. Follow every rule below exactly; the core is driven by automated checks, and the rules below are the contract they check. Where the rules leave something open, decide, keep it consistent everywhere, and write it down.

# 1. Files and boundaries

- `package.json` exists (type module); add a "test" script so `npm test` runs every test with node:test. No dependencies of any kind, no build step.
- `src/` holds the core (pure JavaScript, no DOM, no timers, no randomness other than the seeded generator below) and the renderer. The core must run in Node; the renderer only in the browser.

# 2. Random numbers (`src/rng.js`)

`createRng(seed)` returns a generator implementing mulberry32 over the 32-bit unsigned seed `seed >>> 0`:

```
next(): state = (state + 0x6D2B79F5) >>> 0; t = state; t = Math.imul(t ^ (t >>> 15), t | 1); t ^= t + Math.imul(t ^ (t >>> 7), t | 61); return ((t ^ (t >>> 14)) >>> 0) / 4294967296;
```

`next()` returns a float in [0, 1); `int(max)` returns `Math.floor(next() * max)` (an integer in [0, max)); `pick(array)` returns `array[int(array.length)]`; `state` is readable and writable (the 32-bit unsigned number, always kept in that range), so a game can serialize it and restore it. For seed 123 the first three `next()` values are 0.7872516233474016, 0.1785435655619949, 0.49531551403924823.

# 3. Levels (`src/map.js`)

`generateLevel(seed, depth)` returns `{ width, height, tiles, rooms, start, stairs }`:

- `width` is 60 and `height` is 30. `tiles` is an array of `height` strings of `width` characters: `#` wall, `.` floor, `>` stairs down. Every tile on the outer border is a wall.
- Between 6 and 12 rooms: `rooms` is an array of `{ x, y, w, h }` describing rectangles of floor tiles (w and h between 3 and 10). Rooms never touch: for any two rooms there is at least one wall tile between them in every direction (the rectangles enlarged by one tile do not overlap). Rooms are connected by corridors of floor tiles.
- Every floor tile (and the stairs) is reachable from `start` by 8-directional movement over non-wall tiles.
- `start` is a floor tile inside the first room; `stairs` is a tile inside another room: the room whose centre `(x + w / 2, y + h / 2)` is farthest from `start` (Euclidean distance; the first such room in `rooms` on a tie). For depth below 5 the stairs tile is `>`; on depth 5 (the last one) there is no `>` anywhere and `stairs` is a plain floor tile where the Amulet lies.
- The same seed and depth always produce the identical level; generation uses only `createRng(seed)`.

Passable tiles are `.` and `>`. Everything else in this document that says "adjacent" or "step" means the 8 neighbouring tiles (Chebyshev distance 1), diagonals included, with no corner-cutting rule.

# 4. Field of view (`src/fov.js`)

`computeFov(tiles, x, y, radius)` returns a Set of strings `"x,y"` of the visible tiles, defined exactly like this: a tile T is visible from the origin O when its Euclidean distance satisfies dx*dx + dy*dy <= radius*radius and every tile on the Bresenham line from O to T, excluding T itself, is not a wall. The origin is always visible. Walls are visible when the line reaches them. The Bresenham line is the integer algorithm:

```
dx = |x1 - x0|; dy = -|y1 - y0|; sx = x0 < x1 ? 1 : -1; sy = y0 < y1 ? 1 : -1; err = dx + dy;
loop: visit (x0, y0); if (x0 == x1 && y0 == y1) stop; e2 = 2 * err; if (e2 >= dy) { err += dy; x0 += sx; } if (e2 <= dx) { err += dx; y0 += sy; }
```

# 5. Pathfinding (`src/path.js`)

`findPath(tiles, from, to, blocked = [])` returns the shortest path from `from` to `to` as an array of `{ x, y }` steps, excluding the start and including the target, moving 8-directionally over passable tiles; `blocked` is a list of `{ x, y }` tiles that count as impassable (except the target itself). It returns `null` when there is no path. Any shortest path is acceptable; its length must be minimal.

# 6. The game (`src/game.js`)

`createGame(options)` creates a game. `options.seed` (integer, default 1) seeds everything. Without a fixture the game generates depth 1 with `generateLevel(levelSeed(seed, 1), 1)` where `levelSeed(seed, depth) = (seed + depth * 7919) >>> 0`, places the player at `start`, and populates the level (section 8). With a fixture the level is exactly what the caller says: `options.map` is an array of row strings (any size, same characters), `options.player` is `{ x, y }`, `options.monsters` is an array of `{ type, x, y }`, `options.items` an array of `{ kind, x, y, amount? }`; a fixture level gets no generated monsters or items and no stairs unless the map contains `>`.

`game.state` is a plain, JSON-serialisable object with at least these fields (extra fields are allowed):

```
{ seed, depth, turn, status,             // status: "playing" | "dead" | "won"
  width, height, tiles,                   // tiles: array of row strings
  visible, explored,                      // visible: array of "x,y" strings; explored: array of row strings of "0"/"1"
  player: { x, y, hp, maxHp, attack, defense, level, xp, gold, inventory, equipment: { weapon, armor } },
  monsters: [ { id, type, x, y, hp, maxHp, attack, defense, xp } ],
  items: [ { id, kind, x, y, amount } ],  // amount only for gold
  log }                                   // array of strings, the most recent last, at most 50 kept
```

The player starts with hp 30, maxHp 30, attack 5, defense 1, level 1, xp 0, gold 0, an empty inventory and no equipment. `visible` is recomputed after every action with `computeFov` from the player's tile with radius 8; `explored` marks every tile that has ever been visible.

`game.act(action)` performs one player action; when the action costs a turn, `turn` increases by one and then every monster takes its turn (section 7). It returns the array of log messages the action produced. Actions:

- `{ type: "move", dx, dy }` with dx, dy in -1..1, not both 0. Into a passable tile with no monster: the player moves (costs a turn). Into a monster: the player attacks it (costs a turn). Into a wall or off the map: nothing happens, no turn, a message such as "There is a wall in the way."
- `{ type: "wait" }`: costs a turn.
- `{ type: "pickup" }`: picks up the items on the player's tile. Gold is never stored: it adds `amount` to `player.gold` (message "You pick up N gold."). The Amulet ends the game: status becomes "won", message "You found the Amulet of Yendor! You win." Every other item goes to the inventory as `{ kind, name }`, which holds at most 10 items; an item that does not fit stays on the floor with the message "Your pack is full." The action costs a turn when at least one item was picked up. With nothing on the tile: no turn, message "There is nothing here."
- `{ type: "use", index }`: uses inventory item `index` (0-based). A potion heals 10 hp, capped at maxHp, and is consumed. A weapon or armor is equipped into the matching slot; the item previously in that slot, if any, returns to the inventory. Costs a turn. An invalid index: no turn, a message.
- `{ type: "drop", index }`: moves the inventory item to the floor at the player's tile (costs a turn). Invalid index: no turn.
- `{ type: "descend" }`: only on a `>` tile; otherwise no turn and a message. On the stairs: depth increases by one, the new level is `generateLevel(levelSeed(seed, depth), depth)` populated per section 8, the player stands on its `start`, visible and explored start over, turn continues counting; the message is "You descend to depth N." It costs a turn, so the new level's monsters act once (none of them starts next to the player).

When status is not "playing", `act` changes nothing and returns [].

Combat is deterministic. The player's effective attack is `attack` plus the equipped weapon's bonus (dagger 1, sword 3); effective defense is `defense` plus the equipped armor's bonus (leather 1, chain 2). Damage dealt = max(1, attacker's effective attack - defender's effective defense). A monster whose hp reaches 0 or less is removed, the player gains its xp, message "You kill the <type>." (before that, "You hit the <type> for N."). A monster attacking the player: message "The <type> hits you for N."; when the player's hp reaches 0 or less, hp is 0, status becomes "dead", message "You die."

Levels: after gaining xp, while `xp >= threshold(level + 1)` with `threshold(L) = 5 * L * (L - 1)` (level 2 at 10 xp, level 3 at 30, level 4 at 60, level 5 at 100): level increases by one, maxHp increases by 5, hp increases by 5 (capped at the new maxHp), attack increases by 1, message "Welcome to level N."

`game.serialize()` returns a JSON string; `loadGame(json)` returns a game whose state and future behaviour are identical to the original (include the rng state). `game.hash()` returns a string: FNV-1a 32-bit hash, as 8 lowercase hex digits, of `JSON.stringify` of the state with every object's keys sorted recursively.

`applyKey(game, key)` maps one key to an action and performs it, returning the messages, or `null` for a key that is not an action: h j k l y u b n move (h left, l right, k up, j down, y up-left, u up-right, b down-left, n down-right; up means y - 1), `.` wait, `g` pickup, `>` descend, digits `1`..`9` use inventory item 0..8. `runScript(game, text)` applies the characters of `text` in order, skipping whitespace and unknown characters.

# 7. Monsters

| type | hp | attack | defense | xp | sight |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| rat | 4 | 2 | 0 | 3 | 5 |
| goblin | 8 | 3 | 1 | 6 | 6 |
| skeleton | 12 | 4 | 2 | 10 | 6 |
| orc | 18 | 6 | 2 | 15 | 7 |
| troll | 30 | 8 | 3 | 30 | 7 |

After each turn-costing player action, monsters act in increasing `id` order, one step or attack each. A monster adjacent to the player attacks. Otherwise, when the player's tile is in `computeFov` from the monster's tile with the monster's sight radius, it takes one step along `findPath` toward the player, treating other monsters as blocked; when no path exists it stays. Otherwise it wanders: with probability one half it stays, else it moves to a random adjacent passable tile that holds no monster and not the player, chosen with the game's rng. Monsters never share a tile with each other or with the player and never enter walls.

# 8. Populating a generated level

On a generated level of depth d: 3 + 2d monsters, each of a type chosen with the rng from the types allowed at that depth (depth 1: rat, goblin; depth 2: rat, goblin, skeleton; depth 3: goblin, skeleton, orc; depth 4: skeleton, orc; depth 5: orc, troll), placed on distinct floor tiles outside the first room. 3 + d items on distinct floor tiles that hold no monster and are not the player's tile: each item is a potion with probability 0.4, gold with 0.3 (amount = 5 + int(16) coins), else one of dagger, sword, leather, chain with equal probability. On depth 5 an additional item of kind "amulet" lies on the level's `stairs` tile. Item ids and monster ids are unique within the game.

# 9. The page and the renderer

`index.html` plus `src/main.js` (a module) and whatever renderer modules you like:

- URL parameters: `seed` (integer) fixes the seed; `script` is a key string applied with `runScript` before the first frame. When either parameter is present the title screen is skipped and the game starts at once; otherwise a title screen with the game's name and controls waits for any key and the seed is random.
- A HUD element with id `hud` whose text contains `HP 30/30`, `Depth 1` and `Turn 0` at the start of a new game (and the current values afterwards), the player's level, xp and gold. A message log element with id `log` showing the last messages. An inventory panel toggled with `i`, listing items by number.
- Keyboard: the keys of section 6, plus arrow keys for the four directions, `R` to restart after death or victory, `?` for help. Death and victory screens.
- The renderer is three.js: floor tiles, walls with height, the stairs, the player and each monster type as distinct low-poly meshes or coloured shapes with a glyph label, items as small shapes; unexplored tiles are not drawn, explored tiles outside the current view are dimmed, visible tiles are lit; a light follows the player; the camera looks down at the player from above and behind and follows smoothly; a hit flashes the target and shakes the screen briefly, a kill spawns a short particle burst; monsters and the player move with a short tween rather than teleporting. A dark palette with a few strong accent colours. Optional: WebAudio beeps for hits and pickups.
- Expose the game as `window.game` for debugging.

# 10. Tests and documentation

Every core module has node:test tests in `test/`; cover generation constraints, field of view, paths, combat numbers, items, levels, stairs, serialization and determinism (the same seed and script give the same hash). Write a README.md: how to play, the controls, the architecture (modules, the state shape, how the renderer reads the state), and how to run the tests. npm test must pass.

- `renderer.js` — `handleEvents` handles `{ type: 'rewind' }` with a 250 ms cyan `fx.screenFlash` (alpha 0.28), a small `fx.burst` of 14 cyan particles at the player's restored tile, and a brief cool flash on the player mesh; no shake, so it never reads as a hit. `handleEvents` takes the state as an internal second argument (the exported `createRenderer` interface is unchanged), and unknown events are still ignored exactly as before.
- `renderer.js` + `effects.js` — fixed one real stale-view bug: a cut arriving while a previous fade-in is still running (which is the rewind-of-a-descend case) used to be ignored for the rest of that fade, leaving the stale level painted for roughly 400 ms. The cut condition now allows an in-flight fade-in to be interrupted and `startFadeOut()` resumes from the current opacity rather than snapping. A same-level rewind still never fades, because neither the level key nor `restartPending` changes.

**Verification:** `npm test` passes (132/132), and every capture reported zero console messages and zero page errors. The kill case is the clearest: `?seed=4&script=bjn` shows the rat alive beside the player, `bjnn` kills it (particles, XP 3), and `bjnnz` has it back on its restored tile with XP 0, hp 29 and the restored log. The descend case: the 59-move script lands on the stairs at Depth 1, adding `>` switches to Depth 2, and adding `>z` reproduces the pre-descend frame exactly — previous level rebuilt, no fade, no stale level. The cue captures show the cyan pulse over the already-restored state.

One caveat worth your attention: a `script` URL is applied before the first frame and diffed in bulk by `src/main.js`, so a scripted `z` emits no `rewind` event and no capture can show the cue from the page's own path; the cue captures were produced with a temporary, clearly marked trigger that I then removed (a fresh URL confirms it is gone). The event itself is emitted for interactive `z` presses, which is the path the cue was built for.

project.goal:
Build DELVE, a turn-based roguelike, in this repository: a deterministic game core in plain JavaScript (ES modules, Node 22+, no dependencies) with its own tests, and a 3D renderer for the browser built on three.js. Follow every rule below exactly; the core is driven by automated checks, and the rules below are the contract they check. Where the rules leave something open, decide, keep it consistent everywhere, and write it down.

# 1. Files and boundaries

- `package.json` exists (type module); add a "test" script so `npm test` runs every test with node:test. No dependencies of any kind, no build step.
- `src/` holds the core (pure JavaScript, no DOM, no timers, no randomness other than the seeded generator below) and the renderer. The core must run in Node; the renderer only in the browser.
- `index.html` at the root loads three.js from exactly this URL with a plain script tag: `https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/three.js/0.160.0/three.min.js` (the global `THREE`). Nothing else is loaded from the network. The page loads `src/main.js` as a module script with a relative path and must work from a file:// URL in Chrome started with `--allow-file-access-from-files` (the screenshot tool and the checks do that) or from any static file server; no build step, no bundler.
- Never use eval, new Function, node:vm, child_process, or dynamic code loading. The core modules (rng, map, fov, path, game) must not read the clock or Math.random; the page may use Math.random only to pick the seed of a new game.
- A custom tool named `screenshot` is available in this project: it opens an HTML file in headless Chrome, returns a screenshot and the page's console messages and errors. Use it whenever you change the page or the renderer; a page with console errors is not done.

# 2. Random numbers (`src/rng.js`)

`createRng(seed)` returns a generator implementing mulberry32 over the 32-bit unsigned seed `seed >>> 0`:

```
next(): state = (state + 0x6D2B79F5) >>> 0; t = state; t = Math.imul(t ^ (t >>> 15), t | 1); t ^= t + Math.imul(t ^ (t >>> 7), t | 61); return ((t ^ (t >>> 14)) >>> 0) / 4294967296;
```

`next()` returns a float in [0, 1); `int(max)` returns `Math.floor(next() * max)` (an integer in [0, max)); `pick(array)` returns `array[int(array.length)]`; `state` is readable and writable (the 32-bit unsigned number, always kept in that range), so a game can serialize it and restore it. For seed 123 the first three `next()` values are 0.7872516233474016, 0.1785435655619949, 0.49531551403924823.

# 3. Levels (`src/map.js`)

`generateLevel(seed, depth)` returns `{ width, height, tiles, rooms, start, stairs }`:

- `width` is 60 and `height` is 30. `tiles` is an array of `height` strings of `width` characters: `#` wall, `.` floor, `>` stairs down. Every tile on the outer border is a wall.
- Between 6 and 12 rooms: `rooms` is an array of `{ x, y, w, h }` describing rectangles of floor tiles (w and h between 3 and 10). Rooms never touch: for any two rooms there is at least one wall tile between them in every direction (the rectangles enlarged by one tile do not overlap). Rooms are connected by corridors of floor tiles.
- Every floor tile (and the stairs) is reachable from `start` by 8-directional movement over non-wall tiles.
- `start` is a floor tile inside the first room; `stairs` is a tile inside another room: the room whose centre `(x + w / 2, y + h / 2)` is farthest from `start` (Euclidean distance; the first such room in `rooms` on a tie). For depth below 5 the stairs tile is `>`; on depth 5 (the last one) there is no `>` anywhere and `stairs` is a plain floor tile where the Amulet lies.
- The same seed and depth always produce the identical level; generation uses only `createRng(seed)`.

Passable tiles are `.` and `>`. Everything else in this document that says "adjacent" or "step" means the 8 neighbouring tiles (Chebyshev distance 1), diagonals included, with no corner-cutting rule.

# 4. Field of view (`src/fov.js`)

`computeFov(tiles, x, y, radius)` returns a Set of strings `"x,y"` of the visible tiles, defined exactly like this: a tile T is visible from the origin O when its Euclidean distance satisfies dx*dx + dy*dy <= radius*radius and every tile on the Bresenham line from O to T, excluding T itself, is not a wall. The origin is always visible. Walls are visible when the line reaches them. The Bresenham line is the integer algorithm:

```
dx = |x1 - x0|; dy = -|y1 - y0|; sx = x0 < x1 ? 1 : -1; sy = y0 < y1 ? 1 : -1; err = dx + dy;
loop: visit (x0, y0); if (x0 == x1 && y0 == y1) stop; e2 = 2 * err; if (e2 >= dy) { err += dy; x0 += sx; } if (e2 <= dx) { err += dx; y0 += sy; }
```

# 5. Pathfinding (`src/path.js`)

`findPath(tiles, from, to, blocked = [])` returns the shortest path from `from` to `to` as an array of `{ x, y }` steps, excluding the start and including the target, moving 8-directionally over passable tiles; `blocked` is a list of `{ x, y }` tiles that count as impassable (except the target itself). It returns `null` when there is no path. Any shortest path is acceptable; its length must be minimal.

# 6. The game (`src/game.js`)

`createGame(options)` creates a game. `options.seed` (integer, default 1) seeds everything. Without a fixture the game generates depth 1 with `generateLevel(levelSeed(seed, 1), 1)` where `levelSeed(seed, depth) = (seed + depth * 7919) >>> 0`, places the player at `start`, and populates the level (section 8). With a fixture the level is exactly what the caller says: `options.map` is an array of row strings (any size, same characters), `options.player` is `{ x, y }`, `options.monsters` is an array of `{ type, x, y }`, `options.items` an array of `{ kind, x, y, amount? }`; a fixture level gets no generated monsters or items and no stairs unless the map contains `>`.

`game.state` is a plain, JSON-serialisable object with at least these fields (extra fields are allowed):

```
{ seed, depth, turn, status,             // status: "playing" | "dead" | "won"
  width, height, tiles,                   // tiles: array of row strings
  visible, explored,                      // visible: array of "x,y" strings; explored: array of row strings of "0"/"1"
  player: { x, y, hp, maxHp, attack, defense, level, xp, gold, inventory, equipment: { weapon, armor } },
  monsters: [ { id, type, x, y, hp, maxHp, attack, defense, xp } ],
  items: [ { id, kind, x, y, amount } ],  // amount only for gold
  log }                                   // array of strings, the most recent last, at most 50 kept
```

The player starts with hp 30, maxHp 30, attack 5, defense 1, level 1, xp 0, gold 0, an empty inventory and no equipment. `visible` is recomputed after every action with `computeFov` from the player's tile with radius 8; `explored` marks every tile that has ever been visible.

`game.act(action)` performs one player action; when the action costs a turn, `turn` increases by one and then every monster takes its turn (section 7). It returns the array of log messages the action produced. Actions:

- `{ type: "move", dx, dy }` with dx, dy in -1..1, not both 0. Into a passable tile with no monster: the player moves (costs a turn). Into a monster: the player attacks it (costs a turn). Into a wall or off the map: nothing happens, no turn, a message such as "There is a wall in the way."
- `{ type: "wait" }`: costs a turn.
- `{ type: "pickup" }`: picks up the items on the player's tile. Gold is never stored: it adds `amount` to `player.gold` (message "You pick up N gold."). The Amulet ends the game: status becomes "won", message "You found the Amulet of Yendor! You win." Every other item goes to the inventory as `{ kind, name }`, which holds at most 10 items; an item that does not fit stays on the floor with the message "Your pack is full." The action costs a turn when at least one item was picked up. With nothing on the tile: no turn, message "There is nothing here."
- `{ type: "use", index }`: uses inventory item `index` (0-based). A potion heals 10 hp, capped at maxHp, and is consumed. A weapon or armor is equipped into the matching slot; the item previously in that slot, if any, returns to the inventory. Costs a turn. An invalid index: no turn, a message.
- `{ type: "drop", index }`: moves the inventory item to the floor at the player's tile (costs a turn). Invalid index: no turn.
- `{ type: "descend" }`: only on a `>` tile; otherwise no turn and a message. On the stairs: depth increases by one, the new level is `generateLevel(levelSeed(seed, depth), depth)` populated per section 8, the player stands on its `start`, visible and explored start over, turn continues counting; the message is "You descend to depth N." It costs a turn, so the new level's monsters act once (none of them starts next to the player).

When status is not "playing", `act` changes nothing and returns [].

Combat is deterministic. The player's effective attack is `attack` plus the equipped weapon's bonus (dagger 1, sword 3); effective defense is `defense` plus the equipped armor's bonus (leather 1, chain 2). Damage dealt = max(1, attacker's effective attack - defender's effective defense). A monster whose hp reaches 0 or less is removed, the player gains its xp, message "You kill the <type>." (before that, "You hit the <type> for N."). A monster attacking the player: message "The <type> hits you for N."; when the player's hp reaches 0 or less, hp is 0, status becomes "dead", message "You die."

Levels: after gaining xp, while `xp >= threshold(level + 1)` with `threshold(L) = 5 * L * (L - 1)` (level 2 at 10 xp, level 3 at 30, level 4 at 60, level 5 at 100): level increases by one, maxHp increases by 5, hp increases by 5 (capped at the new maxHp), attack increases by 1, message "Welcome to level N."

`game.serialize()` returns a JSON string; `loadGame(json)` returns a game whose state and future behaviour are identical to the original (include the rng state). `game.hash()` returns a string: FNV-1a 32-bit hash, as 8 lowercase hex digits, of `JSON.stringify` of the state with every object's keys sorted recursively.

`applyKey(game, key)` maps one key to an action and performs it, returning the messages, or `null` for a key that is not an action: h j k l y u b n move (h left, l right, k up, j down, y up-left, u up-right, b down-left, n down-right; up means y - 1), `.` wait, `g` pickup, `>` descend, digits `1`..`9` use inventory item 0..8. `runScript(game, text)` applies the characters of `text` in order, skipping whitespace and unknown characters.

# 7. Monsters

| type | hp | attack | defense | xp | sight |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| rat | 4 | 2 | 0 | 3 | 5 |
| goblin | 8 | 3 | 1 | 6 | 6 |
| skeleton | 12 | 4 | 2 | 10 | 6 |
| orc | 18 | 6 | 2 | 15 | 7 |
| troll | 30 | 8 | 3 | 30 | 7 |

After each turn-costing player action, monsters act in increasing `id` order, one step or attack each. A monster adjacent to the player attacks. Otherwise, when the player's tile is in `computeFov` from the monster's tile with the monster's sight radius, it takes one step along `findPath` toward the player, treating other monsters as blocked; when no path exists it stays. Otherwise it wanders: with probability one half it stays, else it moves to a random adjacent passable tile that holds no monster and not the player, chosen with the game's rng. Monsters never share a tile with each other or with the player and never enter walls.

# 8. Populating a generated level

On a generated level of depth d: 3 + 2d monsters, each of a type chosen with the rng from the types allowed at that depth (depth 1: rat, goblin; depth 2: rat, goblin, skeleton; depth 3: goblin, skeleton, orc; depth 4: skeleton, orc; depth 5: orc, troll), placed on distinct floor tiles outside the first room. 3 + d items on distinct floor tiles that hold no monster and are not the player's tile: each item is a potion with probability 0.4, gold with 0.3 (amount = 5 + int(16) coins), else one of dagger, sword, leather, chain with equal probability. On depth 5 an additional item of kind "amulet" lies on the level's `stairs` tile. Item ids and monster ids are unique within the game.

# 9. The page and the renderer

`index.html` plus `src/main.js` (a module) and whatever renderer modules you like:

- URL parameters: `seed` (integer) fixes the seed; `script` is a key string applied with `runScript` before the first frame. When either parameter is present the title screen is skipped and the game starts at once; otherwise a title screen with the game's name and controls waits for any key and the seed is random.
- A HUD element with id `hud` whose text contains `HP 30/30`, `Depth 1` and `Turn 0` at the start of a new game (and the current values afterwards), the player's level, xp and gold. A message log element with id `log` showing the last messages. An inventory panel toggled with `i`, listing items by number.
- Keyboard: the keys of section 6, plus arrow keys for the four directions, `R` to restart after death or victory, `?` for help. Death and victory screens.
- The renderer is three.js: floor tiles, walls with height, the stairs, the player and each monster type as distinct low-poly meshes or coloured shapes with a glyph label, items as small shapes; unexplored tiles are not drawn, explored tiles outside the current view are dimmed, visible tiles are lit; a light follows the player; the camera looks down at the player from above and behind and follows smoothly; a hit flashes the target and shakes the screen briefly, a kill spawns a short particle burst; monsters and the player move with a short tween rather than teleporting. A dark palette with a few strong accent colours. Optional: WebAudio beeps for hits and pickups.
- Expose the game as `window.game` for debugging.

# 10. Tests and documentation

Every core module has node:test tests in `test/`; cover generation constraints, field of view, paths, combat numbers, items, levels, stairs, serialization and determinism (the same seed and script give the same hash). Write a README.md: how to play, the controls, the architecture (modules, the state shape, how the renderer reads the state), and how to run the tests. npm test must pass.
